stem: Pre-generics containers stored object. The runtime cost of getting an int back out was:
options: A cast that can THROW at run time, after compiling fine
explanation: (int)box.Item compiles whatever Item holds - and explodes with InvalidCastException in front of the user. Generics move that error to compile time.

stem: In class Box<T>, what is T?
options: A PLACEHOLDER filled in by whoever uses the class - Box<string>, Box<int>...
explanation: One class definition, every type, full compile-time safety: words.Item.Length works because the compiler KNOWS it is a string.

stem: Calling First(new[] {3, 1, 2}) without writing First<int> works because:
options: The compiler INFERS T from the argument
explanation: Type inference reads T from what you pass - which is why you have called dozens of generic methods without noticing they were generic.

stem: Why does calling item.CompareTo(best) inside Largest<T> fail WITHOUT a constraint?
options: T could be ANY type, and not every type has CompareTo
explanation: Unconstrained T only promises object's members. 'where T : IComparable<T>' narrows T in exchange for the capability.

stem: To write 'new T()' inside a generic method you need:
options: where T : new() - a public parameterless constructor
explanation: Each constraint unlocks an ability: new() for construction, IComparable for ordering, a base class for its members.

stem: List<int> beats the old ArrayList because:
options: The runtime generates an int-specialised version - real ints, NO boxing, no casts
explanation: For value types, generics are specialised at runtime: safer AND faster with no trade-off. 6.2 measures what boxing costs.

stem: static T First<T>(T[] items) => items[0]; is a:
options: Generic METHOD - its own type parameter, independent of any class
explanation: Methods can be generic on their own. The <T> after the name declares it; usage rarely needs to spell it out.

stem: Pair<TFirst, TSecond> shows that generic types may:
options: Take SEVERAL type parameters, conventionally named descriptively
explanation: Dictionary<TKey, TValue> and Func<T, TResult> follow the same convention: T alone when single, TDescriptive when several.

stem: Which of these is NOT built on generics?
explanation: Nullable, Task, Func, IEnumerable, the collections - generics run through the whole platform. WriteLine is plain overloading.

stem: SimpleStack<T> was ~20 lines and works for every type ever. The lesson's point:
options: There is NO MAGIC in Stack<T> - generics let one small class serve all types safely
explanation: Push/Pop over a doubling array plus one type parameter = the real collection, unpolished. 5.6 finishes the job.
